bull_bear.body: Dividend resumed: INR 14/share (100% of FY26 FCF distributed); Policy: Progressive distribution of FCF subject to working capital/debt targets; No minimum payout fixed; Debt levels maintained prudently despite net cash position.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body: Geopolitical supply chain disruptions (West Asia war) affecting tower inputs; Customer concentration (Bharti/Vi); Aging portfolio maintenance costs; Regulatory RoW delays (mitigated by new incentive schemes); Africa execution risk.
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Confident on cash flows and 5G momentum; Cautious on near-term supply chain and maintenance seasonality; Committed to progressive dividends; Long-term view on Africa.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body: Q4 maintenance spike is seasonal/portfolio age-driven, not a structural reset; Churn/exit spike in H2 is BAU relocation for safety/landlord issues, not tenant loss; Smart meter mandate (CEA 2026) will enable granular billing and further energy cost optimization.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- India's largest telecom tower company by number of towers and co-locations operated
- Shared-infrastructure model lowers capital intensity for telecom-operator customers, supporting long-term contracts and customer stickiness
- Nationwide footprint across all 22 telecom circles with a substantial market share in customers' rollouts
- Distributed solar footprint (42K+ solar sites) and energy-transition focus supporting operating efficiency and sustainability
- First-mover international diversification into Nigeria, Uganda and Zambia leveraging existing operational expertise and an anchor customer relationship
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Customer concentration / tenant financial risk — Tower companies typically depend on a limited number of large telecom operators as tenants; any financial stress, consolidation, or strategic shift by key tenants can impact revenues and growth. Operators also face significant capital commitments toward spectrum, network investments and regulatory dues (including AGR instalments), which may constrain their ability to meet obligations and sustain network expansion at the same pace.
- Regulatory and policy risk — Telecom infrastructure remains subject to a complex regulatory environment of approvals, permits and local compliance requirements; while reforms such as the RoW Rules, 2024 aim to streamline deployment, implementation may vary across regions, potentially delaying site rollout, and evolving sustainability-related requirements may add further compliance obligations over time.
- TSP consolidation impact on infrastructure sharing — The benefits of passive infrastructure sharing are closely linked to the number of active telecom operators in the market; continued sector consolidation may reduce the scope for co-location and shared infrastructure usage, impacting tenancy growth and limiting the economics of the shared-infrastructure model.
- Contract renewal risk — Renegotiation of long-term customer contracts presents a potential risk to future revenues; as agreements approach renewal there is risk of customer exit or changes to pricing structures, escalation clauses and commercial terms, which could impact revenue visibility and profitability.
- Environmental and energy risk — Tower operations are energy-intensive and exposed to power-availability and cost headwinds; dependence on diesel generators in regions with unreliable grid supply raises operating costs and carbon emissions, rising fuel prices and evolving environmental regulation may further affect cost structures, and extreme weather events (cyclones, floods, heatwaves) pose risks to infrastructure integrity and service continuity.
- Operational and execution risk — Managing a large, geographically dispersed portfolio of tower sites involves site acquisition, permitting and lease-negotiation challenges that can be time-consuming and subject to local constraints; security risks such as battery theft, fuel pilferage and vandalism (particularly in remote areas) can disrupt operations, and delays in rollout or maintenance can affect service quality and customer satisfaction.
- Technological and competitive disruption risk — Increased adoption of active network sharing among operators could reduce the need for separate tenancies, and non-terrestrial networks such as satellite broadband may offer alternative connectivity in certain use cases (particularly remote regions); separately, the growing use of small cells and lean towers may let smaller, more agile players deploy faster and cheaper, exerting pricing pressure on established tower companies.
- EMF compliance and public perception risk — Telecom towers are subject to stringent EMF exposure norms among the most conservative globally, regularly monitored through regulatory audits and inspections, with non-compliance attracting penalties and potential site shutdown; despite adherence to standards, public perception and local opposition in certain areas may still pose challenges to site acquisition and network expansion.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body: Macro Towers: 264,500 (+6.1% YoY); Co-locations: 428,000 (+5.6% YoY); Tenancy Ratio: Stable at 1.62; Lean Towers: 14,000+; IBS/DAS: Leadership position gained in Q4, pickup in metros/tunnels.

latest_quarter.title: Margins & cost dynamics

outlook.body: Revenue: High single-digit organic growth expected (7-7.5% adjusted); Margin: Targeting 55%+ annually despite seasonal Q4 maintenance spikes; Order Inflow: Strong 5G densification demand; Capex: ~70% growth-oriented (towers), ~25% maintenance, Africa capex initially negligible.
outlook.title: Guidance

outlook.body: Robust India order book driven by 5G rollout and network expansion of key customers; Africa orders initial/anchor stage (Zambia license secured, Uganda/Nigeria pending).
outlook.title: Order book & pipeline

outlook.body: Africa expansion (Zambia, Uganda, Nigeria) as long-term frontier; 5G data traffic growth (40% of total traffic) driving incremental loading on existing assets; Green energy services monetization.
outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Strategy anchored in four core pillars: increasing market share, driving cost efficiency, ensuring high network uptime, and advancing sustainability
- International expansion into Africa (Nigeria, Uganda, Zambia) via a calibrated approach starting with greenfield tower deployments, leveraging the anchor-customer presence of Bharti Airtel, with intent to expand into additional markets over time
- Growth in adjacent business lines: achieved leadership position in In-Building Solutions (IBS) via a proactive acquisition strategy; scaling Distributed Antenna System (DAS) deployments across metros, tunnels and highways; continued focus on build-to-suit solutions
- Digital transformation agenda using AI, automation, advanced analytics, digital twins and IoT to improve uptime, field execution, real-time asset visibility and data-led decision-making
- Cost-efficiency programme centred on digital tools, standardised processes, stronger governance frameworks, field productivity and value-engineering-led capex design optimisation
- Structured decarbonisation pathway aligned to a net-zero ambition for 2050, including scaling solar integration and lithium-ion battery adoption to reduce diesel dependency
- The Board recommended/declared a final dividend of INR 14 per equity share for FY26, put to Members for approval at the 20th AGM. On the capex side, management describes a disciplined capital-allocation approach: strengthened investment discipline through standardised evaluation frameworks, improved material utilisation, and enhanced procurement efficiencies across deployments, alongside a shift to more efficient technologies (e.g., lithium-ion over lead-acid batteries).
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Domestic footprint stood at 264,514 macro towers and 428,014 co-locations across 22 telecommunication circles as on March 31, 2026, plus 14,044 co-locations on lean towers. The Company is expanding into adjacent telecom infrastructure segments, including In-Building Solutions (IBS, ~1.7K colocations) across enterprise, institutional and public-infrastructure segments, and Distributed Antenna System (DAS) deployments across metros, tunnels and highways. It has also taken its first step into international expansion, incorporating a wholly owned subsidiary (Indus Towers FZE) in the UAE along with three step-down subsidiaries, and step-down subsidiaries in Nigeria, Uganda and Zambia, identified as priority African markets for a phased, calibrated entry (initial greenfield tower deployments) with intent to expand into additional markets over time.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- 5G rollout maturing into densification and capacity-augmentation phase, expected to drive incremental tower demand via additional equipment loading, site upgrades and selective new tower deployments
- Vodafone Idea's gradual normalisation of network investments — supported by a Board-approved potential fundraise of up to INR 200 billion and Government restructuring of AGR dues (staggered repayment to 2041) — expected to be a meaningful driver of incremental infrastructure demand
- Continued 4G expansion by certain operators to close coverage gaps expected to further support demand for new sites, co-locations and amendments
- Rural connectivity gap (rural tele-density ~60.5% vs urban 151.5%) represents a substantial long-term addressable opportunity, supported by Government programmes such as BharatNet Phase III
- Low fibre penetration at tower sites (~46%) against a National Telecom Policy 2025 target of ~80% fiberisation by 2030 implies a large addressable backhaul/fiberisation opportunity as 5G requires materially higher backhaul capacity
- Favourable regulatory environment — RoW Rules 2024 operationalised across 33 states/UTs and Green Energy Open Access policy notified in 28 states — reducing deployment friction and lowering energy costs
- August 2025 Apex Court ruling (Commissioner, CGST vs. Bharti Airtel) reaffirming telecom towers as movable property, making input tax credit admissible, is a positive for sector economics and tax efficiency
- Continued monetisation improvement via calibrated operator pricing actions (e.g., withdrawal of entry-level prepaid plans) expected to support gradual ARPU improvement even without a formal tariff hike
- Commercial frameworks with the anchor customer (Bharti Airtel) have been established and initial orders are in place across the Africa expansion markets (Nigeria, Uganda, Zambia), with operating licenses secured in all three; rollout activity expected to commence and gather momentum during FY27
outlook.title: Demand & outlook drivers

deepdive.thesis: Indus Towers delivered solid Q4FY26 growth driven by 5G-led co-location additions and improved customer health, while resuming dividends (INR 14/share) signaling cash flow confidence despite near-term margin pressure from seasonal maintenance and geopolitical supply chain headwinds. The strategic pivot to Africa and aggressive green energy adoption structurally lower long-term opex, offsetting aging portfolio maintenance costs.

risks.note: Tower companies typically depend on a limited number of large telecom operators as tenants; any financial stress, consolidation, or strategic shift by key tenants can impact revenues and growth. Operators also face significant capital commitments toward spectrum, network investments and regulatory dues (including AGR instalments), which may constrain their ability to meet obligations and sustain network expansion at the same pace.

Telecom infrastructure remains subject to a complex regulatory environment of approvals, permits and local compliance requirements; while reforms such as the RoW Rules, 2024 aim to streamline deployment, implementation may vary across regions, potentially delaying site rollout, and evolving sustainability-related requirements may add further compliance obligations over time.

risks.risk: TSP consolidation impact on infrastructure sharing
risks.note: The benefits of passive infrastructure sharing are closely linked to the number of active telecom operators in the market; continued sector consolidation may reduce the scope for co-location and shared infrastructure usage, impacting tenancy growth and limiting the economics of the shared-infrastructure model.

Renegotiation of long-term customer contracts presents a potential risk to future revenues; as agreements approach renewal there is risk of customer exit or changes to pricing structures, escalation clauses and commercial terms, which could impact revenue visibility and profitability.

Tower operations are energy-intensive and exposed to power-availability and cost headwinds; dependence on diesel generators in regions with unreliable grid supply raises operating costs and carbon emissions, rising fuel prices and evolving environmental regulation may further affect cost structures, and extreme weather events (cyclones, floods, heatwaves) pose risks to infrastructure integrity and service continuity.

Managing a large, geographically dispersed portfolio of tower sites involves site acquisition, permitting and lease-negotiation challenges that can be time-consuming and subject to local constraints; security risks such as battery theft, fuel pilferage and vandalism (particularly in remote areas) can disrupt operations, and delays in rollout or maintenance can affect service quality and customer satisfaction.

Increased adoption of active network sharing among operators could reduce the need for separate tenancies, and non-terrestrial networks such as satellite broadband may offer alternative connectivity in certain use cases (particularly remote regions); separately, the growing use of small cells and lean towers may let smaller, more agile players deploy faster and cheaper, exerting pricing pressure on established tower companies.

risks.risk: EMF compliance and public perception risk
risks.note: Telecom towers are subject to stringent EMF exposure norms among the most conservative globally, regularly monitored through regulatory audits and inspections, with non-compliance attracting penalties and potential site shutdown; despite adherence to standards, public perception and local opposition in certain areas may still pose challenges to site acquisition and network expansion.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: India's largest telecom passive infrastructure company, providing shared towers and co-locations to all major wireless telecom service providers nationwide.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Indus Towers deploys, owns, operates and manages passive telecom infrastructure (towers, co-locations, dark fibre, duct space, Right-of-Way) which it leases/rents to telecom service providers on a shared, long-term contract basis. It has a pan-India presence across all 22 telecom circles (36 states/UTs) and, during FY26, began an international expansion into Nigeria, Uganda and Zambia through subsidiaries.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- 5G rollout maturing into densification and capacity-augmentation phase, expected to drive incremental tower demand via additional equipment loading, site upgrades and selective new tower deployments
- Vodafone Idea's gradual normalisation of network investments — supported by a Board-approved potential fundraise of up to INR 200 billion and Government restructuring of AGR dues (staggered repayment to 2041) — expected to be a meaningful driver of incremental infrastructure demand
- Continued 4G expansion by certain operators to close coverage gaps expected to further support demand for new sites, co-locations and amendments
- Rural connectivity gap (rural tele-density ~60.5% vs urban 151.5%) represents a substantial long-term addressable opportunity, supported by Government programmes such as BharatNet Phase III
- Low fibre penetration at tower sites (~46%) against a National Telecom Policy 2025 target of ~80% fiberisation by 2030 implies a large addressable backhaul/fiberisation opportunity as 5G requires materially higher backhaul capacity
- Favourable regulatory environment — RoW Rules 2024 operationalised across 33 states/UTs and Green Energy Open Access policy notified in 28 states — reducing deployment friction and lowering energy costs
- August 2025 Apex Court ruling (Commissioner, CGST vs. Bharti Airtel) reaffirming telecom towers as movable property, making input tax credit admissible, is a positive for sector economics and tax efficiency
- Continued monetisation improvement via calibrated operator pricing actions (e.g., withdrawal of entry-level prepaid plans) expected to support gradual ARPU improvement even without a formal tariff hike
- Commercial frameworks with the anchor customer (Bharti Airtel) have been established and initial orders are in place across the Africa expansion markets (Nigeria, Uganda, Zambia), with operating licenses secured in all three; rollout activity expected to commence and gather momentum during FY27

margins.body: Energy margin improved to -3.6% (from -5.2% YoY) via solar/battery mix; Q4 EBITDA impacted by seasonal maintenance (Q3/Q4 focus) and aging portfolio strengthening; Cost per tower structurally down over 3-4 years despite absolute cost rise from volume.

It has also taken its first step into international expansion, incorporating a wholly owned subsidiary (Indus Towers FZE) in the UAE along with three step-down subsidiaries, and step-down subsidiaries in Nigeria, Uganda and Zambia, identified as priority African markets for a phased, calibrated entry (initial greenfield tower deployments) with intent to expand into additional markets over time.

- Nationwide footprint across all 22 telecom circles with a substantial market share in customers' rollouts

themes.title: Telecom & digital-infrastructure capex
themes.need: 5G monetization, FTTH and tower/fibre densification drive the connectivity cycle - and Q1FY27 repriced the optical leg outright. STLTECH booked order intake of INR 13,100cr in ONE quarter, 1.7x its entire FY26 order book, anchored by a multi-year $1.1bn hyperscaler deal running through FY29, taking the open order book to INR 18,618cr (up 2.4x QoQ) on revenue of INR 1,910cr (+87%) and EBITDA INR 397cr (+184%). It then raised guidance twice on the same call - EBITDA margin target from 20%-by-end-FY27 (already hit at 20.8% in Q1) to 23%, and Data-Center + Enterprise mix from 30% to 50% of FY27 revenue, after DC went from 1% of revenue in FY26 to 21%. The catch is supply, not demand: ex the anchor deal quarterly intake fell to ~INR 3,000cr from INR 7,000-8,000cr because 'we have to pick and choose the orders basis the capacity availability', with germanium and helium named as binding raw-material constraints. BHARTIARTL on ARPU + 5G; INDUSTOWER on tower rollout; SUYOG-tier on passive infra; GTPL/HFCL-tier on broadband + fibre; tariff hikes and rural FTTH are the near-term levers.
themes.driver: STLTECH's $1.1bn hyperscaler ramp against germanium/helium supply constraints and the raised 23% margin / 50% DC-mix guides; tariff-hike flow-through; 5G/FTTH capex; tower tenancy adds.
